newsitem.title: UK: Abbey bid turns up pressure on ScotAm.
newsitem.headline: Abbey bid turns up pressure on ScotAm.

text.p: Directors at mutually-owned Scottish Amicable are in danger of missing out on a 14 million pound ($22.45 million) payday if a surprise bid by Abbey National bid for the life assurance group on Friday succeeds.

Just two weeks after ScotAm outlined a two stage proposal to drop mutual status and float the group on the stock market, Abbey National unveiled a 1.4 billion pound offer, which, industry analysts said, may prove difficult for policyholders to resist.

"The original proposals have not been enthusisatically received and certainly following the Abbey approach it's unlikely policyholders wiil vote in favour of them. The odds are in favour of ScotAm being taken over by somebody," said one.
Under ScotAm's plans 12 directors stand to share around 14 million pounds if growth targets of 25 percent annually are met.

ScotAm's 2,200 employees were also included in an incentive scheme which the management said was necessary to change the culture of the company to make it more profit-oriented, aggressive and efficient.
But the payouts have been heavily criticised and contrast with the relatively meagre benefits likely to accrue to the 1.1 million with-profits policyholders, who own the company.
Today's Abbey bid includes an immediate 400 million pound minimum payout to policyholders in cash or Abbey shares.
That compares with an initial 75 million pounds on demutualisation and further benefits at flotation worth at least 200 million pounds under ScotAm's proposals.
But instead of cash, that bonus is in the form of extra policy bonuses and policyholders will have to wait until policies mature before getting the money.
Analysts said the Abbey bid had been astutely pitched and was likely to be attractive to policyholders.
"It's more money and it's more money up front and therefore guaranteed money," said one.
Despite assertions by the company that it was keen to hold on to its independence the Abbey offer raises the possibility of a bidding war developing.
Should that occur Abbey would be heavily favoured to win after its Scottish Mutual purchase in 1991.

"Abbey do look the favourite - parts of the business can be put together (with Scottish Mutual) to achieve cost economies. In another sense they would be a welcome predator since they would keep the jobs in Scotland," said another analyst.

ScotAm, the country's sixth largest mutual, was maintaining on Friday that the actual payout to policyholders under its proposals was likely to be worth more than the 200 million pound headline figure.

"The 200 million pound flotation value' quoted by Abbey National is in fact the minimum value to be realised for the policyholders interest in new business opperations. The actual value of the new business operations is expected to be substantially higher," the company said in a statement.

ScotAm chairman Sandy Stewart said Abbey National's offer which he described as "vague" and "inadequate" had not been dismissed out of hand and that the interests of policyholders were uppermost in the management's mind.

No discussions have been held between the two groups and ScotAm said it had no intention of talking to the Abbey ahead of the release of details on its demutualisation, due within the next two weeks. ($1=.6237 Pound)
